Legal Issues & MHCA 2017

Legal issues in mental health — the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, admission, discharge, rights, informed consent and the nurse’s role.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • Describe the Mental Healthcare Act 2017
  • Explain types of mental health admission
  • List the rights of the mentally ill
  • Apply consent and confidentiality in psychiatric care

In simple words

The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 replaced the Mental Health Act, 1987. It protects the rights of people with mental illness and gives them the right to access mental health care with dignity.

Types of admission

Type Who decides
Independent admission A patient who can decide for themselves stays by choice
Supported admission For patients with limited capacity; all admissions are supported under the Act
Emergency admission Up to 72 hours when there is immediate danger

Rights under MHCA 2017

  • Right to access mental health care
  • Right to equality and non-discrimination
  • Right to live in the community
  • Right to be free from cruel, inhuman treatment
  • Right to keep their property
  • Right to an advance directive — a written instruction about treatment preferences
  • Right to confidentiality and records
  • Right to legal aid and to challenge decisions

Other legal points

  • Attempted suicide is decriminalised under MHCA 2017 — the person must be treated and supported
  • Consent must be informed and, where possible, by the patient
  • Restraint and seclusion are regulated; chains and beatings are forbidden
  • Discharge requires a review and family involvement for supported admissions
  • Confidentiality of the record is required, with limits for safety
  • Mental Health Review Boards review admissions and grievances

🔴 Suicide is a treatment matter, not a crime

Under the Mental Healthcare Act 2017, attempted suicide must be treated as an emergency for care, not an offence. Nurses must respond, protect and refer.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. MHCA 2017 replaces the Mental Health Act, 1987.
  2. Admission types: independent, supported and emergency (72 hours).
  3. Advance directive records the patient’s treatment preference.
  4. Restraint must be authorised, monitored and never physical punishment.
  5. Attempted suicide must be treated, not criminalised.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Patients have the right to live in the community.
  2. Mental Health Review Boards hear complaints.
  3. Informed consent is needed for ECT and other procedures.
  4. Medical records must be kept confidential.
  5. Discharge plans must involve family and follow-up.

📌 Memory trick

Admission: I-S-E — Independent, Supported, Emergency.

60-second revision

  • MHCA 2017 replaced MHA 1987.
  • Admission: independent, supported, emergency (72 hours).
  • Rights: access, community living, dignity, property, records, legal aid.
  • Advance directive guides future treatment.
  • Nurses: take consent, document, avoid illegal restraint, support discharge.

Test yourself

In India, a patient with limited capacity is admitted under:

Answer: B. A supported admission is for patients who need support to decide, with a nominated representative.

The Mental Healthcare Act was passed in:

Answer: C. The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 replaced the Mental Health Act, 1987.

An emergency psychiatric admission may be made for how long:

Answer: B. Emergency admission is permitted for up to 72 hours when there is immediate danger.

An advance directive is:

Answer: B. An advance directive records the patient’s own preference about future mental health treatment.

A person who has attempted suicide must be:

Answer: B. Under MHCA 2017, attempted suicide requires care and support, not punishment.
